name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q01 - Neural organisation in animals and PNS divisions

questiontext.text:
Match the neural structures or divisions in List I with their corresponding features in List II.

List IList II
A. Hydra(i) Brain present along with ganglia and neural tissues
B. Insects(ii) Transmits impulses from CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles
C. Somatic neural system(iii) Simple network of neurons
D. Autonomic neural system(iv) Relays impulses from CNS to skeletal muscles

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animal neural organisation increases in complexity from lower invertebrates to vertebrates, and the human peripheral neural system (PNS) is functionally divided into somatic and autonomic divisions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
In lower invertebrates such as Hydra, the neural organisation is very simple and composed of a network of neurons, so A pairs with (iii).
In insects, the neural system is better organised with a brain along with a number of ganglia and neural tissues, so B pairs with (i).
The somatic neural system relays impulses from the central neural system (CNS) to skeletal muscles, so C pairs with (iv).
The autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles, so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q02 - Types of neurons and myelin sheath gaps

questiontext.text:
Match the neuronal types or structures in List I with their correct descriptions or locations in List II.

List IList II
A. Multipolar neuron(i) Cell body with one axon only; usually embryonic stage
B. Bipolar neuron(ii) One axon and two or more dendrites; cerebral cortex
C. Unipolar neuron(iii) Gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths
D. Nodes of Ranvier(iv) One axon and one dendrite; retina of eye

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neurons are classified into multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar types based on the number of axons and dendrites, while myelinated axons feature periodic gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Multipolar neurons have one axon and two or more dendrites and are found in the cerebral cortex, so A pairs with (ii).
Bipolar neurons possess one axon and one dendrite and are found in the retina of the eye, so B pairs with (iv).
Unipolar neurons have a cell body with one axon only and are usually found in the embryonic stage, so C pairs with (i).
The gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths formed by Schwann cells around myelinated axons are called nodes of Ranvier, so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q03 - Ionic events during resting potential and impulse conduction

questiontext.text:
Match the electrophysiological states or mechanisms in List I with their corresponding ionic events in List II.

List IList II
A. Resting axonal membrane(i) Active transport of \(3\,\text{Na}^+\) outwards for \(2\,\text{K}^+\) into the cell
B. Sodium-potassium pump(ii) Rapid influx of \(\text{Na}^+\) reversing membrane polarity
C. Depolarisation at stimulated site(iii) Diffusion of \(\text{K}^+\) outside restoring resting potential
D. Repolarisation(iv) Comparatively more permeable to \(\text{K}^+\) and nearly impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Generation and conduction of a nerve impulse depend on selective ion permeability of the axonal membrane, active ion transport, and rapid sequential changes in \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{K}^+\) permeability.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
When a neuron is resting, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to \(\text{K}^+\) and nearly impermeable to \(\text{Na}^+\), so A pairs with (iv).
Ionic gradients across the resting membrane are maintained by the sodium-potassium pump, which actively transports \(3\,\text{Na}^+\) outwards for \(2\,\text{K}^+\) into the cell, so B pairs with (i).
When a stimulus is applied, the site becomes freely permeable to \(\text{Na}^+\), causing rapid \(\text{Na}^+\) influx and reversal of polarity (depolarisation), so C pairs with (ii).
Immediately afterwards, \(\text{K}^+\) permeability rises and \(\text{K}^+\) diffuses outside the membrane within a fraction of a second to restore the resting potential (repolarisation), so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(iv), B-(i), C-(ii), D-(iii).

questiontext.text:
Match the protective or connective structures of the human brain in List I with their anatomical descriptions in List II.

List IList II
A. Dura mater(i) Very thin middle layer of cranial meninges
B. Arachnoid(ii) Tract of nerve fibres connecting left and right cerebral hemispheres
C. Pia mater(iii) Outer layer of cranial meninges
D. Corpus callosum(iv) Inner layer of cranial meninges in contact with brain tissue

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inside the skull, the human brain is covered by three protective cranial meninges, and its two cerebral hemispheres are interconnected by a major commissural fibre tract.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Dura mater is the outer layer of the cranial meninges, so A pairs with (iii).
Arachnoid is the very thin middle layer of the cranial meninges, so B pairs with (i).
Pia mater is the inner layer that lies directly in contact with the brain tissue, so C pairs with (iv).
Corpus callosum is the tract of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres, so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

questiontext.text:
Match the brain regions in List I with their primary regulatory or integrative functions in List II.

List IList II
A. Association areas(i) Control body temperature and urge for eating and drinking
B. Thalamus(ii) Complex functions like intersensory associations, memory, and communication
C. Hypothalamus(iii) Control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, and gastric secretions
D. Medulla oblongata(iv) Major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Distinct regions of the forebrain and hindbrain are specialised for higher-order integration, sensory-motor relay, homeostatic drives, and vital autonomic reflexes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Association areas of the cerebral cortex are neither clearly sensory nor motor, and are responsible for complex functions such as intersensory associations, memory, and communication, so A pairs with (ii).
The thalamus, wrapped around by the cerebrum, acts as a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling, so B pairs with (iv).
The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus and contains centres controlling body temperature as well as the urge for eating and drinking, so C pairs with (i).
The medulla oblongata of the hindbrain contains centres that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, and gastric secretions, so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q06 - Midbrain brain stem and reflex arc components

questiontext.text:
Match the neural structures in List I with their corresponding anatomical features or roles in List II.

List IList II
A. Cerebral aqueduct(i) Four round swellings on the dorsal portion of midbrain
B. Corpora quadrigemina(ii) Transmits impulse via dorsal nerve root into CNS
C. Brain stem(iii) Canal passing through the midbrain
D. Afferent neuron in reflex arc(iv) Formed by midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The midbrain and brain stem form critical anatomical links between the forebrain, hindbrain, and spinal cord, while the spinal reflex arc routes sensory input through the dorsal root.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
A canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain, so A pairs with (iii).
The dorsal portion of the midbrain consists mainly of four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina, so B pairs with (i).
Three major regions—midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata—make up the brain stem, so C pairs with (iv).
In a reflex arc, the afferent neuron receives a signal from a sensory organ and transmits the impulse via a dorsal nerve root into the CNS, so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q07 - Olfactory bulb and layers of human eyeball

questiontext.text:
Match the sensory structures in List I with their descriptions in List II.

List IList II
A. Olfactory bulb(i) Bluish middle layer of eyeball containing many blood vessels
B. Sclera(ii) External layer of eyeball composed of dense connective tissue
C. Choroid(iii) Pigmented, opaque continuation of ciliary body regulating pupil diameter
D. Iris(iv) Pair of broad bean-sized extensions of the brain's limbic system

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Olfactory reception connects directly to extensions of the limbic system, while the wall of the human eyeball consists of three layers with specialised anterior modifications.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Neurons of the olfactory epithelium extend directly into a pair of broad bean-sized organs called olfactory bulbs, which are extensions of the brain's limbic system, so A pairs with (iv).
The external layer of the eyeball, composed of dense connective tissue, is the sclera, so B pairs with (ii).
The middle layer of the eyeball is the choroid, which contains many blood vessels and appears bluish, so C pairs with (i).
The ciliary body continues forward to form the pigmented and opaque iris, whose muscle fibres regulate the diameter of the pupil, so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(iv), B-(ii), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q08 - Photoreceptors and fluid chambers of the eye

questiontext.text:
Match the ocular structures in List I with their corresponding functions or contents in List II.

List IList II
A. Cones(i) Twilight (scotopic) vision; contain rhodopsin
B. Rods(ii) Space between lens and retina filled with transparent gel
C. Aqueous chamber(iii) Daylight (photopic) vision and colour vision
D. Vitreous chamber(iv) Space between cornea and lens containing thin watery fluid

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The retina houses two types of photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) for different light intensities and colour perception, while the eyeball interior is divided into two fluid-filled chambers by the lens.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Daylight (photopic) vision and colour vision are functions of cones, which respond to red, green, and blue lights, so A pairs with (iii).
Twilight (scotopic) vision is the function of rods, which contain the purplish-red protein rhodopsin (a derivative of Vitamin A), so B pairs with (i).
The space between the cornea and the lens is the aqueous chamber, containing a thin watery fluid called aqueous humor, so C pairs with (iv).
The space between the lens and the retina is the vitreous chamber, filled with a transparent gel called vitreous humor, so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_NEURAL_CONTROL_AND_COORDINATION_MATCH_Q09 - Auditory and vestibular structures of the ear

questiontext.text:
Match the structures of the human ear in List I with their specific locations or functions in List II.

List IList II
A. Eustachian tube(i) Projecting ridge in ampulla of semicircular canals
B. Organ of Corti(ii) Connects middle ear with pharynx to equalise pressure
C. Crista ampullaris(iii) Sensory projecting ridge of saccule and utricle
D. Macula(iv) Located on basilar membrane; contains auditory hair cells

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The middle and inner ear contain specialised structures for pressure equalisation, auditory transduction, and maintenance of body balance and posture.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity with the pharynx and helps equalise pressures on either side of the ear drum, so A pairs with (ii).
The organ of Corti is located on the basilar membrane of the cochlea and contains hair cells acting as auditory receptors, so B pairs with (iv).
The swollen base (ampulla) of each semicircular canal contains a projecting ridge with hair cells called the crista ampullaris, so C pairs with (i).
The saccule and utricle of the otolith organ contain a sensory projecting ridge called the macula, so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these pairs gives the correct matching sequence: A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).
